newsitem.title: UK: Children dying from hunger in N. Korea - UNICEF.
newsitem.headline: Children dying from hunger in N. Korea - UNICEF.

text.p: Thousands of children and babies in North Korea are severely malnourished and some die from lack of food every day, a senior official of the United Nations Children's Fund said on Friday after a four-day visit to the country.

Marie Staunton, deputy director of UNICEF in Britain, said at one nursery she visited, she saw only 18 listless and emaciated five-year-olds, severely malnourished with sunken eyes and protruding ribs.

"Children are dying. They are dying every day," Staunton told Reuters. "They look like wizened old men. It tears your heart out. They've just got no energy and they don't smile. That's when you know how serious the situation is."
International aid agencies have estimated that 80,000 children in the country suffer from severe malnutrition and a total of 800,000 from some degree of undernurishment.

UNICEF has targeted much of its relief efforts on supplying high energy milk for children and training doctors and nurses to administer it properly. The agency has already delivered 105 metric tonnes of the "miracle milk" and three further plane loads with the same amount are to land in the capital Pyongyang next week.
"The milk really works. You can actually see a child improve in a matter of days or weeks. That's the encouraging part. If we can just get enough supplies there, they can be saved," Staunton said.
Two years of devastating floods and a severe drought has plunged the country into a dire food crisis with nearly 70 percent of North Korea's crops wiped out and its food stocks emptied.
As she and her colleagues were driven through the countryside, they saw ghost-like highways devoid of traffic because the country has nearly run out of fuel.

When UNICEF first sent in a plane full of emergency supplies, the agency found it could not distribute the aid because the trucks had no petrol. For its subsequent deliveries, the organisation brought in its own fuel from Singapore.

The only traffic the group encountered was lorries full of soldiers and ragged families, including children, heading for the parched fields in a desperate attempt to plant a second crop before the onset of winter.

The famine began in 1995 when floods ruined arable land, crops, fertiliser stores and irrigation systems. A recent drought, which lasted more than 60 days, destroyed 1.5 million tonnes of maize expected to cover the country's food needs between from November 1997 to October 1998.
As the crisis worsens, four-nation talks between China, the United States, North and South Korea on proposed peace negotiations for the divided Korean peninsula stalled in New York on Thursday.
The talks are to resume on September 15 to continue work on the logistics for talks aimed at replacing the fraying 1950-53 Korean War armistice with a more durable peace agreement.
